key_terms.def: An instructor-to-learner assessment, oral, written or both, used with traditional or authentic assessment, one on one or in a class; it belongs right after the performance [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].
The current AIH word for what the PTS calls evaluation: it shows how, what and how well a learner is learning [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
Sympathy or over-identification with a learner to a degree that it influences the instructor's objectivity [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].
A fact question relies on recall and asks who, what, when or where; a HOTS question asks why or how and makes the learner analyze, solve problems and draw conclusions [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].
Open-ended questions, usually starting with why or how, draw full answers; closed-ended ones can be answered yes or no and check only the rote level [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
A reply to a learner's question that returns the question to the same learner to answer [[25:214|AIH G-6]].
The extent to which a test measures what it is supposed to measure; the most important consideration in test evaluation [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].
Words in a test item, such as always and never, that give a clue to the answer [[25:210|AIH G-2]].
Grading learners against a carefully written, measurable standard rather than against each other [[25:210|AIH G-2]].
Skill testing, desirable for evaluating training that involves an operation, a procedure or a process; the ACS/PTS practical tests are criterion-referenced performance tests [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

FAA standards that must be met for a certificate or rating [[25:209|AIH G-1]] [[25:213|AIH G-5]]. The PTS tests through oral or written questions and demonstrated skill; the ACS evaluates knowledge, risk management and skill elements for each task [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.2]] [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.3]].
Learner centered grading: a learner self-assessment and a detailed instructor assessment, followed by a discussion that compares the two [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

chunks.title: From PTS words to today's AIH words

body.p: The PTS Task asks you to explain two things, critique and evaluation, and it lists FAA-H-8083-9 as the reference (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I, Task E). The PTS also tells users to work from the current edition of each reference (FAA-S-8081-9E, references NOTE). The current Aviation Instructor's Handbook, FAA-H-8083-9B, treats both ideas in one chapter called Assessment, and it says learner where the PTS says student [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.D (Student Evaluation, Assessment, and Testing) covers the same chapter from the CFI ACS side and goes deeper on the rubrics; this lesson follows the PTS outline item by item and adds how to explain each item to an examiner.

body.p: **Evaluation versus critique.** The AIH keeps the two apart in its chapter on learning. In the first stages of a skill, practical suggestions are worth more to the learner than a grade. Early evaluation mostly serves the teacher: it checks teaching effectiveness, helps predict learner outcomes and locates special problem areas, and the same observations reveal the strengths and weaknesses you need to know before you can criticize constructively [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. Letting learners critique their own performance makes the training more learner-centered [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. Put simply (application): evaluation tells where the learner stands, and critique helps the learner get better. An assessment should give the learner direction and guidance to raise the level of performance [[25:132|AIH 6-1]], and it is pointless unless the learner benefits from it [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

The AIH pictures evaluation as three tools: knowledge tests, oral quizzes and performance tests, and assessment can happen before, during and after training [[25:106|AIH 5-3]]. Formal assessments, such as a quiz or written exam, are documented; informal ones, which can include verbal critique, happen as needed and are not part of the final grade [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

callout.text: Application: on the checkride, say the PTS word first, then the current one: 'The PTS calls it a critique; the current handbook treats the critique as an instructor-to-learner assessment [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].' Evaluators are told to test your application and correlation skills (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction), and linking the two vocabularies is a quick way to show correlation.

check.q: An examiner asks what 'evaluation' in the PTS Task means today. How do you answer in current AIH terms?
check.a: It is assessment: finding out how, what and how well a learner is learning. Flight instructors generally use the review, collaborative assessment (LCG), written tests and performance-based tests [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

body.p: **Purpose of an effective critique.** The critique is an instructor-to-learner assessment, used with traditional or authentic assessment, one on one or in a class [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. The word can sound negative, and you must not use it as a chance to be overly critical. An effective critique looks at good as well as bad performance, the individual parts, how the parts relate and the overall performance, so it is as varied as the performance itself [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

head: Who it serves
What the critique does
rows: The learner
Shows how well he or she is progressing, with practical, specific feedback and direction on how to raise the level of performance [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
The learner
Most important: a chance for self-evaluation, which builds aeronautical decision-making and judgment [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
You
Immediate feedback on the quality of your instruction [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
You
Shows where to put more emphasis: if several learners stumble at the same step, you need a better explanation, another demonstration or special emphasis [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]

body.p: **When and how.** A critique may be oral, written or both. It should come immediately after the performance, while the details are easy to recall. You may critique any activity a learner performs or practices, privately or before a whole class [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. Put the postflight critique in written form, such as notes, so you cover every area you noticed during the flight or lesson [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

**Make the purpose clear.** Learners who do not understand the purpose of an assessment are unlikely to accept it, and little improvement follows [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Plan the ending too: the principle of recency is why instructors plan a summary for a postflight critique and restate the important points at the end [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

callout.text: One line for the examiner: a critique should give the learner direction to raise the level of performance [[25:132|AIH 6-1]], not be a chance to be overly critical [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

check.q: An applicant tells the examiner that the purpose of a critique is to list every mistake so the learner never repeats them. What is missing?
check.a: A critique should give direction to raise the learner's level of performance [[25:132|AIH 6-1]] without being overly critical, covering good as well as bad performance, the parts and the whole [[25:141|AIH 6-10]], and it should give the learner a chance to self-evaluate [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

body.p: **Characteristics of an effective critique.** To give direction and raise the learner's performance, an assessment has to be factual and line up with the lesson's completion standards [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]. The AIH lists eight characteristics of effective assessment; use them to answer the PTS item [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

head: Characteristic
What the AIH says
Ask yourself before you speak (application)
rows: Objective

Based on the facts of the performance as they were, not as they could have been. Likes, dislikes, biases and personality conflicts can bend it; sympathy or over-identification is halo error [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Would I give the same grade to a learner I find difficult?
Flexible
Judge the whole performance in its context; good learners sometimes perform poorly and poor learners well. Fit tone, technique and content to the occasion and the learner [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
What should I say, omit, stress and minimize today? [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Acceptable
The learner must have confidence in your qualifications, teaching ability, sincerity, competence and authority; a certificate alone rarely does it [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]
Am I speaking fairly, with conviction, from competence the learner can see?
Comprehensive
Not necessarily long. Covers strengths and weaknesses in proportion to the situation [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Do a few major points or several minor ones help more? [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Constructive
Praise builds on what went well; every weakness gets positive guidance; praise for its own sake and comments that point nowhere are left out [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Does each fault I name come with a fix?
Organized
Any logical pattern the learner can follow [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Which pattern fits this flight? (see below)
Thoughtful
Respects the learner's need for self-esteem, recognition and approval; no ridicule, anger or fun at the learner's expense; criticism in private when possible [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Who else is listening?
Specific
Says why and how to improve. At the end the learner knows what went well, what went poorly and specifically how to improve [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Could the learner act on this on the next flight?

body.p: **Four ways to organize it.** The patterns are the AIH's [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]; the instrument examples are application:

bullets: Follow the sequence of the performance itself [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]: departure, en route, hold, approach, missed approach.

Start at the point where the performance failed and work backward through the steps that led to it; a success can be analyzed the same way [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. Example: from the moment the approach went a dot high back to a late descent at the fix.
Build the whole critique around one glaring deficiency [[25:134|AIH 6-3]], such as an approach flown without a briefing.
Break the whole into parts, or build the parts into a whole [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

callout.text: Application memory aid for the eight, in order: Our Flight Always Comes Clean Only Through Specifics. Objective, Flexible, Acceptable, Comprehensive, Constructive, Organized, Thoughtful, Specific [[25:133|AIH 6-2]] [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

check.q: You rated your favorite learner's sloppy hold 'good' because she worked so hard. Which characteristic did you break, and what is the error called?
check.a: Objectivity. Sympathy or over-identification with a learner that influences objectivity is halo error; assess the performance as it was [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

body.p: **Methods for a critique.** The AIH gives six ways to conduct one, usable one on one or in a classroom [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. Name all six for the examiner, then say which you would use and why.

head: Method
How it works
Your control point
rows: Instructor/learner critique
You lead a group discussion and invite class members to offer criticism of a performance [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Control it carefully, give it a clear purpose and keep it organized, never a random free-for-all [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Learner-led critique
A learner leads; you may set the pattern and techniques or leave them to the leader [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
May not be efficient because the participants are inexperienced, but can generate interest and learning [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Small group critique
Small groups each analyze one assigned area and present their findings; the combined reports can make a comprehensive assessment [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Furnish the criteria and guidelines [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Individual learner critique by another learner
Another learner presents the whole assessment, or you ask several learners about the manner and quality of the performance [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Discussion helps the group take ownership of the ideas; keep firm control [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Self-critique
The learner critiques his or her own performance [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
It still gets your control and supervision [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Written critique
Written by you, or by every learner about one performance [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Gains: more time and thought, a record the learner keeps, and every classmate's suggestions for the performer. Drawback: the rest of the class does not benefit [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]

body.p: **One-on-one flight training.** Most CFII teaching is one on one, so the self-critique carries the weight. As a learner grows in flight knowledge, he or she should be able to lead the postflight review while you guide the discussion with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. The guided discussion method works in preflight and postflight briefings as well as in class [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. In flight training the learner's self-assessment is the first of the two parts of collaborative assessment, covered later in this lesson [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

callout.text: Application: in a ground school class, a written critique pairs well with a short instructor/learner discussion. The performer keeps the written record, and the discussion makes up for the written critique's drawback that the class does not benefit [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

check.q: In an evening IFR ground school, one learner gives a practice weather briefing and you want the whole class to learn from the critique. Which method fits, and what is your job during it?
check.a: An instructor/learner critique that you control carefully, direct with a clear purpose and keep organized, not a free-for-all, while avoiding embarrassment to the presenter [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

body.p: **Ground rules for a critique.** The current AIH has no list under that title. It gives the rules for 'whatever the type of critique' on AIH 6-10 [[25:141|AIH 6-10]] and spreads the rest through the book. Gather them into one list you can say aloud:

bullets: **Timing.** Critique immediately after the performance, while the details are easy to recall [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].
**Control.** Keep firm control of any critique with learner participation; a group critique needs a clear purpose and organization [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].
**Settle and correct.** Resolve disagreements and correct erroneous impressions [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].
**Allow for inexperience.** Make allowances for the learners' relative inexperience [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].
**Save time at the end** to cover areas omitted, not emphasized enough, or worth repeating [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].
**Protect the performer.** Avoid embarrassing a learner in front of the class, and deliver criticism in private when you can [[25:141|AIH 6-10]] [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].
**Do not cover everything.** Choose a few major points or a number of minor ones, whichever helps more [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].
**Positive first, positive last.** Make positive comments about progress before the areas that need improving [[25:64|AIH 3-13]], and if possible avoid ending on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
**Explain every error.** Telling an earnest learner the work is unsatisfactory with no explanation causes frustration; brief the errors and how to correct them [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
**Be consistent.** If the same thing is acceptable one day and not the next, the learner gets confused [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
**Praise honestly.** Deserved praise pays dividends, but praise given too freely becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

callout.text: Never invent deficiencies to keep a fast learner humble. Unfair criticism immediately destroys a learner's confidence in the instructor; raise the standard of performance for each lesson instead [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

check.q: Your class critique is running long and ten minutes remain. What does the AIH say to use the end for?
check.a: The areas that were omitted, not emphasized enough, or worth repeating [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

body.p: **Oral assessment** is direct or indirect questioning by the instructor, and it is the most common means of assessment [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. A fact question relies on memory and asks who, what, when or where. A HOTS (higher order thinking skills) question asks why or how and makes the learner combine facts with analysis and problem solving to reach a conclusion [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

Proper quizzing reveals how effective your training methods are, checks retention and comprehension, reviews earlier material, keeps interest and stimulates thinking, emphasizes the important points, finds the points that need more emphasis, and promotes active participation [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

**Characteristics of effective oral questions.** Write pertinent questions in advance, for example in the lesson plan, and add impromptu ones as the lesson develops [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. An effective question must pass five tests [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. The tests are the AIH's; the instrument examples are application:

head: The question must...
Weak
Better
rows: Apply to the subject of instruction
In a holding lesson: 'What are the VFR cloud clearances in Class E?'
'How did you pick your entry for this hold?'
Be brief and concise, but clear and definite
A five-line question about winds, timing, entries and fuel
'Why did your outbound leg come out short?'
Be adapted to the learner's ability, experience and stage of training
Asking a learner on her second hood lesson about RNAV approach design
'Which instrument first showed the nose dropping?'
Center on only one idea (who, what, when, where, how or why, not a combination)
'When do you start down, and what power do you set?'
'When do you start the descent?'
Present a challenge
'Is the approach loaded?'
'What will you do if the GPS loses integrity inside the final approach fix?'

body.p: **Open-ended, not closed-ended.** Open-ended questions, usually starting with why or how, draw full answers from the learner's own knowledge; closed-ended questions can be answered yes or no and check only the rote level [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Since most aviation training is at the understanding level or higher, questions should make learners grasp concepts, explain similarities and differences and infer cause and effect [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]. Phrase them to focus the learner on decision-making and judgment [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

**In a discussion,** a lead-off question opens an area, and a follow-up question brings the discussion back on track or asks for more detail [[25:212|AIH G-4]] [[25:211|AIH G-3]]. An overhead question goes to the whole group; a direct question is aimed at one person [[25:213|AIH G-5]] [[25:210|AIH G-2]]. **In the airplane,** the learner tells, instructor does step lets you check the learner's understanding before he or she has to fly it [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner answers every 'what is' question about approach chart symbols but cannot say why two approaches to the same runway have different minimums. Which kind of question do you add?
check.a: HOTS questions that ask why or how, so the learner has to analyze and draw conclusions instead of only recalling facts [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

chunks.title: Questions to avoid, and how to repair them

body.p: **Types of questions to avoid.** Leave out yes/no questions such as 'Do you understand?' or 'Do you have any questions?' [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. The AIH names six more types to avoid [[25:142|AIH 6-11]] [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. For four of them it gives only an example, so the 'Why it fails' and 'Repair' columns are this lesson's reading, checked against the five characteristics (application).

head: Type
AIH example
Why it fails
Repair
rows: Puzzle
First action for a conventional gear airplane with a weak right brake swerving left in a right crosswind during a full flap, power-on wheel landing [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Piles on conditions, so it is no longer one idea
Ask about one condition at a time
Oversize
'What do you do before beginning an engine overhaul?' [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Too broad to be brief and definite
Narrow it to one step
Toss-up
'In an emergency, should you squawk 7700 or pick a landing spot?' [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Both choices can be right, so it is not definite
Give one case and ask one definite question about it
Bewilderment
A long altimeter question mixing station pressure, temperature, a warm front and mountains [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
The learner cannot tell what is being asked
Split it into short, single questions
Trick question
Options 1, 2, 3 and 4 listed as A. 4, B. 3, C. 2, D. 1. Learners feel they are in a battle of wits with you, and the point of the lesson is lost [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]
Tests reading tricks, not the subject
Test attention to detail with carefully built alternatives instead [[25:200|AIH B-4]]
Irrelevant question
Tire inflation on a test about magneto timing; it brings in unrelated facts and slows progress [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]
Does not apply to the subject of instruction
Ask about the lesson's objective

callout.text: Application: a five-second self-check before you ask: one idea, one question word, fits this learner today, and the learner has to think. If it fails any of these, rewrite it before you say it [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

check.q: You ask a new instrument learner, 'In IMC with a failing vacuum pump, do you fly the airplane or tell ATC?' Which type to avoid is this, and how do you fix it?
check.a: A toss-up, like the AIH's squawk-7700-or-pick-a-landing-spot example [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. Ask one clear question about one situation instead, since an effective question is clear, definite and centers on one idea [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

body.p: **Responses to student questions.** The AIH gives three tips, especially for a classroom [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]:

bullets: Be sure you clearly understand the question before you answer [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. Paraphrasing it back is one way to confirm that you and the learner mean the same thing [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
Show interest in the question and give an answer as direct and accurate as you can [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].
After you answer, find out whether the learner is satisfied with the answer [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

head: Situation
What to do
rows: The full answer is more advanced than the learner needs now
Say it is a good, pertinent question, explain that a detailed answer now would complicate the learning, and invite the learner to ask again at the right point in training [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]
You do not know the answer

Admit it freely and promise to get the answer or, if practical, help the learner look it up [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. Learners sense a bluff quickly, and it destroys their confidence in you [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
The learner can work it out
Use a reverse question: return the question to the same learner to answer [[25:214|AIH G-6]], or direct it to another participant [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]
Before a demonstration
Encourage questions about any step the learner does not understand before you leave the explanation phase [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]
Right after a solo
Debrief at once and answer the learner's questions; with the flight vivid in memory, questions come quickly [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

callout.text: Your answers feed the 'acceptable' test of every later critique: learners must have confidence in your competence and sincerity [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]. One bluffed answer can cost you that [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

check.q: Your learner asks about an autopilot mode you are not sure of. What do you say?
check.a: Admit you do not know, and promise to find the answer or look it up together in the references [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

chunks.title: Effective written tests: characteristics and development

body.p: **Characteristics of an effective written test.** A test is a set of questions, problems or exercises to find out whether the learner has a particular knowledge or skill; each test item measures a single objective and calls for a single response [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]. Written tests check the learner's grasp of information, concepts, terms, processes and rules, the foundation for higher levels of learning [[25:134|AIH 6-3]], and carefully crafted scenario questions can assess higher levels too [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

head: Characteristic
Meaning
How you protect it
rows: Reliability
Consistent results with repeated measurement [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]
Selection items are graded the same whoever grades them; supply items cannot be graded reliably [[25:197|AIH B-1]]. Expect retake scores to rise, because the first test teaches [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]
Validity
Measures what it is supposed to measure; the most important consideration [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]
Have several instructors read it against the objectives, and change or drop items that do not fit [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]
Usability
Easy to give and to grade [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Readable type, clear and concise directions and items, clear graphics [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Objectivity
Singleness of scoring [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
True/false or multiple choice items are much easier to grade objectively than essays [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Comprehensiveness
How well it measures the overall objectives [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Sample a representative cross-section of the objectives, not one cylinder of the engine [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
Discrimination
How well it tells learners apart [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]
A wide range of scores, all levels of difficulty, items that separate levels of achievement. For pilot certification, minimum standards matter far more [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]

body.p: **Development of an effective written test.** The AIH builds a test in four steps that go from general to specific, for knowledge tests and for skill tests alike [[25:138|AIH 6-7]] [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]:

head: Step
What it means
Applied to a presolo test (application)
rows: 1. Determine level-of-learning objectives
A general objective at one level of one domain; it sets the scope [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]
Understanding level: the learner can explain the rules for the home airport's airspace
2. List indicators of desired behaviors
The measurable behaviors that best show the objective was met; sample them, since you cannot measure everything [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]
Answers name the airspace, the radio calls and the weather limits that apply
3. Establish criterion objectives
The behavior, the conditions and the criteria to meet; good performance-based lesson objectives already contain them [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]
Complete the school's presolo test to the passing score your syllabus sets
4. Develop criterion-referenced test items
Items that measure the behaviors in the criterion objective; missed questions show areas not covered well [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]
Cover each area the rule below requires

body.p: A presolo test measures the regulations, the local area, the aircraft type and the procedures to be used, and a test of readiness for a knowledge test should be based on the objectives of all the lessons given [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. By rule, the presolo test covers the applicable sections of parts 61 and 91, the airspace rules and procedures for the solo airport, and the flight characteristics and operational limitations of the make and model [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(b)]].

callout.text: The rule: the student's authorized instructor must administer the presolo knowledge test and, at its conclusion, review all incorrect answers with the student before authorizing solo [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(b)]].

check.q: Several instructors read your new stage test against the course objectives and drop items that do not fit. Which characteristic are they protecting?
check.a: Validity, the extent to which the test measures what it is supposed to measure, the most important consideration [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].

body.p: Good items are hard to write: it takes mastery of the subject, clear writing and the ability to picture realistic situations, so many instructors use commercial test materials, and some keep their own bank of items [[25:197|AIH B-1]]. Supply-type items (a word, sentence or paragraph) let the learner organize and express knowledge but cannot be graded reliably and take longer. Selection-type items are highly reliable, can be machine scored and cover many more areas in a given time [[25:197|AIH B-1]].

**True-false** items suit facts and details with only two possible answers, but they give the greatest probability of guessing and are generally not considered valid [[25:198|AIH B-2]]. If you use them [[25:198|AIH B-2]]:

bullets: One idea per statement, entirely true or entirely false, in your own words rather than verbatim text [[25:198|AIH B-2]].
Avoid unnecessary negatives, and emphasize any negative you must use [[25:198|AIH B-2]].
Avoid ambiguous words (some, generally) and absolutes (all, never, only); absolutes are determiners that give clues to the answer [[25:198|AIH B-2]] [[25:210|AIH G-2]].
Avoid patterns in the order of correct answers, keep statements brief and about the same length, and state the source of a controversial statement [[25:198|AIH B-2]].

body.p: **Multiple choice** items have a stem (the question, statement or problem) and responses; the wrong responses are distractors. They can measure anything from facts to reasoning and application [[25:198|AIH B-2]].

bullets: Three challenges: a clear, unambiguous stem; a correct response that cannot be refuted; and distractors that attract learners who lack the knowledge [[25:199|AIH B-3]].
Prefer a direct question to an incomplete sentence as the stem; it reads more naturally and gives fewer clues [[25:199|AIH B-3]].
Use three or four alternatives, since more than four convincing ones is hard to write. Common learner errors make good distractors [[25:199|AIH B-3]].
For rote-level items, one correct answer and clearly wrong distractors; for higher levels, several acceptable answers with one clearly best, and tell the learner to pick the best [[25:199|AIH B-3]].

Keep items independent, test essential knowledge, emphasize negatives, and avoid double negatives and trick questions. Put only relevant material in the stem and avoid 'a' or 'an' at its end [[25:200|AIH B-4]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.D shows a badly written stem from AIH Figure B-3.
Watch the length: on instructor-made tests the correct alternatives tend to be longer than the wrong ones. List numerical answers in order of size [[25:201|AIH B-5]].

body.p: **Matching** items measure many relationships quickly and reduce guessing, especially if responses can be used more than once. Use closely related material, make every response credible, and prefer unequal columns [[25:201|AIH B-5]].

check.q: You review a colleague's multiple choice quiz and notice the keyed answer is nearly always the longest option. Why does that matter?
check.a: The AIH notes that on instructor-made tests correct alternatives tend to be longer than incorrect ones [[25:201|AIH B-5]]. Application: a test-wise learner can then pick the longest option without knowing the subject, while learners are supposed to select an alternative only if they know it is correct [[25:199|AIH B-3]].

chunks.title: Performance tests and the FAA PTS

body.p: **Characteristics of performance tests.** Performance testing is desirable for evaluating training that involves an operation, a procedure or a process [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. The practical tests are criterion referenced: the objective is for every successful applicant to meet the high standards of knowledge, skill and safety required by the regulations [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Criterion-referenced testing grades learners against a carefully written, measurable standard rather than against each other [[25:210|AIH G-2]].

A good performance test item is content valid, closely mimicking what is required in actual flying, and criterion valid, with completion standards that reflect acceptable standards in actual flight [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Its objective states the behavior, the conditions and the criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]], and in authentic assessment the learner knows the criteria before the assessment [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

**How the PTS is built.** The ACS/PTS sets the standards FAA inspectors and designated examiners use to test for certificates and ratings, and reflects 14 CFR parts 61, 65 and 91, the AIM and pertinent advisory circulars and handbooks [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Areas of operation are phases of the test in a logical sequence; tasks are titles of knowledge areas, procedures or maneuvers; flight instructor applicants are tested on one or more tasks in each area, and required tasks are named in a note after the area title [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. In the CFII PTS, that note requires at least Tasks E, F and G and one other task in Area I (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I NOTE).

bullets: Each Objective lists what the applicant should be able to do, the conditions, the acceptable performance standards and, when applicable, safety considerations (FAA-S-8081-9E, PTS Description).
'Shall' and 'must' are mandatory; 'should' and 'may' are guidance (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

Any Task selected is evaluated in its entirety, and a Task that is incomplete or whose outcome is uncertain must be repeated; that does not permit instruction, practice or repeating an unsatisfactory Task (FAA-S-8081-9E, Use of the PTS and Introduction).

callout.text: The rule: completing a practical test means performing the tasks in the areas of operation of the applicable ACS or PTS [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)(1)]], showing mastery of the aircraft, proficiency and competency within the approved standards, and sound judgment [[60:223|14 CFR 61.43(a)(2)-(4)]]. Failing any area of operation fails the test [[60:223|14 CFR 61.43(c)]].

check.q: The examiner asks what makes the PTS a criterion-referenced test. Your answer?
check.a: Every successful applicant must meet the same published standard instead of being ranked against other applicants [[25:140|AIH 6-9]] [[25:210|AIH G-2]].

chunks.title: Uses of performance tests: from lesson to IPC

body.p: **Uses of the PTS in training.** You do not give the practical test, but your job is to prepare the learner for it, so evaluate each element of the practical test before sending the applicant [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Since evaluators may cover every task, evaluate all tasks before you recommend; the check need not be formal, but it should follow criterion-referenced testing [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

**Not a syllabus.** The ACS/PTS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool; lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed it before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. The certification standards are limited to the most critical job tasks and do not represent an entire training syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

head: Performance test you run
How to run it
rows: Every lesson
Judge demonstrated ability against standards adjusted to the learner's experience and stage, and look at mastery of the elements, not just the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Suspected rote performance
Have the learner vary the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations or apply its elements to other maneuvers [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Before a stage check
Verify the learner meets the proficiency requirements first [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Practical test recommendation
Require a thorough demonstration, never less than the complete procedure in the applicable ACS/PTS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]
Instrument proficiency check (IPC)
Include the tasks in the instrument ACS or PTS task table; you may require any other maneuver you need [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.2]] [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]]

body.p: **The IPC as a CFII's performance test.** To give one, a flight instructor must hold an instrument rating on both the pilot and the flight instructor certificate, appropriate to the category and class of aircraft [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]. Build a plan of action with realistic scenarios [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.3]] and review the criteria for satisfactory completion with the pilot before you start [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.4]]. Afterward, debrief and give a comprehensive analysis with suggestions for any weak areas [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.4]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4]]. If the performance is unsatisfactory, do not endorse it; log the session as dual instruction given [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]].

callout.text: Endorsing a learner for solo, or a pilot for an additional rating, without making sure the regulatory requirements are met is a serious deficiency the FAA may hold you accountable for, and a breach of faith with the learner or applicant [[25:184|AIH 9-14]].

check.q: Your instrument learner flies approaches to standards and asks for a checkride date. What do you do first?
check.a: Evaluate every task in the instrument ACS or PTS against its standards, using criterion-referenced testing, before you recommend him [[25:140|AIH 6-9]] [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

body.p: **Collaborative assessment (or LCG).** The AIH uses both names. Collaborative assessment, or learner centered grading (LCG), is a form of authentic assessment used in aviation training with problem-based learning, and it is used to evaluate whether learning criteria were met during scenario-based training (SBT) [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. With SBT, it is used whenever the learner completes a scenario [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

It has two parts: a learner self-assessment and a detailed assessment by the instructor. The self-assessment is meant to stimulate growth in the learner's thought processes and behaviors; then an in-depth discussion compares your assessment with the learner's [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. The AIH contrasts it with traditional scales such as 'excellent, good, fair, poor', which often meet the instructor's needs but not the learner's [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

The self-assessment follows four open-ended steps, replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect, in what the AIH says might be called a 'collaborative critique' [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.D walks through each step with sample prompts. Through the discussion you and the learner jointly decide the learner's progress, which may be recorded on a rubric [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

head: Rubric
Levels
rows: Maneuvers or procedures
Describe, explain, practice, perform, not observed [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]
Single-pilot resource management (SRM)
Explain, practice, manage-decide [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]

body.p: **Instrument example (application):** after a partial panel approach your learner rates herself Perform. You saw your coaching correct her heading drift twice. On the rubric, needing coaching to correct deviations is Practice, while Perform means she finds and corrects her own errors and the outcome is never in doubt [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Talk it through until she sees the gap, as the AIH's Linda does with Brian [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

bullets: It involves the learner and builds the habit of honest self-assessment a safe pilot needs [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].
The grades describe a level of performance, not prestige, so the learner cannot flunk a lesson [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].
Instructors may think it takes more time, but it is merely a more structured, effective and collaborative version of a traditional postflight critique [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].
Do not force the levels into A to F. Grading is progressive: a task may be a describe item on flight one, practice by flight three and manage-decide by flight five [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

A learner new to self-assessment may be reluctant, so teach the learner how to take part [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Very early in training, before the learner can analyze and evaluate, traditional assessment may be more useful [[25:139|AIH 6-8]].

body.p: **Why the examiner cares.** The PTS lists the ability to use learner-centered grading and debriefing techniques appropriately among the things evaluated, and its definition of instructional knowledge includes the ability to use learner-centered grading (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

check.q: Why does the AIH say a learner cannot 'flunk' a lesson graded this way?
check.a: The grades describe a level of performance, not a level of prestige such as A+, so the learner shows a level of flight and SRM skill instead [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

chunks.title: Risk: how critique and evaluation go wrong

body.p: Each item in this Task can go wrong, and the result is a learner who rejects your feedback, learns the wrong lesson, or thinks he or she is ready and is not. The hazards and the source-backed fixes:

The learner is unlikely to accept it, and little improvement follows [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
State the purpose and the criteria first; learners want to know the criteria they are assessed by [[25:144|AIH 6-13]]

An embarrassed performer [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]

callout.text: Application: the safety tie-in for the examiner. An honest critique and a full evaluation before solo or a checkride are risk controls, and the flight instructor is the only person in a position to decide a learner is ready for solo [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

check.q: A colleague drills learners on a commercial question bank until they score 95 percent. What risk does the AIH name?
check.a: Test prep stresses rote learning; examiners report applicants who passed the knowledge test easily but lacked knowledge in the oral, so use such material only as a supplement to instructor-led training [[25:131|AIH 5-28]].

chunks.title: Explaining this Task to the examiner

body.p: This is a knowledge Task: the objective is to exhibit instructional knowledge by explaining, and instructional knowledge means your explanations follow the teaching procedures and techniques of the AIH (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I Task E and Introduction). Evaluators are told to test application and correlation and to use scenario-based questions when possible (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction), so expect 'Here is a learner who...' more than 'List the...'.
A four-part answer works for any element (application):

bullets: 1. Name it with the PTS word and the current AIH word.
2. Give the AIH list or definition.
3. Give one flight-training example.
4. Say what you would do with a real learner on the next flight.

head: Element
Sample opening line (application)
rows: Critique: purpose and characteristics

'A critique gives the learner direction to raise the level of performance [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]; it is not a chance to be overly critical [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. It must be objective, flexible, acceptable, comprehensive, constructive, organized, thoughtful and specific [[25:133|AIH 6-2]] [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].'
Critique: methods and ground rules

'There are six methods: instructor/learner, learner-led, small group, individual critique by another learner, self-critique and written. Whatever the method, I keep control, settle disagreements and save time at the end [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].'
Oral questions

'An effective question applies to the subject, is brief and clear, fits the learner's stage, centers on one idea and presents a challenge. I avoid yes/no, puzzle, oversize, toss-up, bewilderment, trick and irrelevant questions [[25:142|AIH 6-11]] [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].'
Responses to questions
'I make sure I understand the question, answer directly and accurately, and check that the learner is satisfied. If I don't know, I say so and find out [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].'
Written tests

'A good test is reliable, valid, usable, objective, comprehensive and discriminating [[25:135|AIH 6-4]] [[25:136|AIH 6-5]], and I build it in four steps from objectives to criterion-referenced items [[25:139|AIH 6-8]].'
Performance tests and the PTS
'The PTS is a criterion-referenced performance test [[25:140|AIH 6-9]], a testing document, not a teaching document [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].'
Collaborative assessment
'The learner assesses first, I give my detailed assessment, and we compare the two in a discussion [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].'

body.p: **Role-play.** During the flight portion the evaluator acts as a student during selected maneuvers, and oral questions may come at any time (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Be ready to debrief the examiner as if he or she were your learner: ask for a self-assessment, compare it with yours, and close with specific fixes [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

check.q: The examiner asks you to explain the characteristics of effective oral questions. How do you show application, not just recall?
check.a: Give the five characteristics [[25:142|AIH 6-11]], then turn a weak question from a real lesson into a better one; the PTS tells evaluators to test application and correlation (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).
