scenario.title: Debrief day at the flight school
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII at a Part 61 school. Dev, your instrument learner, is close to his practical test. Today's scenario flight had an IFR departure, a hold and an RNAV approach. He flew the hold and the approach within standards but never briefed the approach, and when you covered the attitude indicator he chased the VSI and lost 200 feet before your coaching got him back. Mia, a newer learner, asks to sit in on the debrief to see how it works. Dev opens with: 'That was basically checkride ready, right?' Later the chief instructor asks you to write a 20-question review test for the school's instrument ground school.

questions.q: How do you open the debrief?
questions.a: With collaborative assessment: Dev assesses himself first, then you compare your assessment with his in an in-depth discussion [[25:176|AIH 9-6]], using replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect to guide him [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. If he has never self-assessed, coach him into it [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

questions.q: Mia is in the room. How do you handle the 200-foot altitude loss?
questions.a: A critique in front of others can help them, but avoid embarrassing the performer [[25:141|AIH 6-10]], and deliver criticism in private when you can [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. Application: ask Dev whether he is comfortable with Mia listening, or save that part until she leaves.

questions.q: Dev rates his partial panel work Perform. You rate it Practice. What now?
questions.a: Your coaching corrected his deviations, which fits Practice; Perform means he finds and corrects his own errors and the outcome is never in doubt [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Talk it through until he sees where he needs more practice, as Linda does with Brian [[25:138|AIH 6-7]], and be specific about what happened, why, and how to fix it [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

Honestly, and with the reason. Before you recommend him, evaluate every task of the instrument ACS or PTS against its standards using criterion-referenced testing [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]; a recommendation never rests on less than the complete procedure [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. The missing approach briefing and the altitude loss are your specific points [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

questions.q: Dev asks a question about his GPS navigator's database that you cannot answer. What do you do?
questions.a: Admit you do not know and promise to find out or look it up together [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. A bluff would cost the confidence that makes your critiques acceptable [[25:133|AIH 6-2]] [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

questions.q: How do you build the 20-question ground school test?
questions.a: Start from the course objectives and work the four steps down to criterion-referenced items [[25:139|AIH 6-8]] [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Base a readiness test on the objectives of all the lessons [[25:140|AIH 6-9]], have other instructors check its validity [[25:135|AIH 6-4]], use selection items for reliability and coverage [[25:197|AIH B-1]], and leave out trick questions [[25:200|AIH B-4]].

skills.do: Explain the critique in PTS order: its purpose, the eight characteristics, the six methods and the ground rules, each with one flight-training example, using both the PTS word 'critique' and the AIH's 'assessment'.
skills.practice: Debrief a friend's practice flight or sim session aloud and have the friend score you on the eight characteristics [[25:133|AIH 6-2]] [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]; then name which of the six methods you used and why [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

skills.do: Explain evaluation: ask and repair oral questions on the spot, answer a learner's question by the three tips, describe how you would build a valid written test, explain the PTS and ACS as criterion-referenced performance tests, and run a short collaborative assessment with the examiner as the learner.
skills.practice: Write five oral questions for one instrument lesson and check each against the five characteristics [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]; draft a ten-item quiz with the four-step process [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]; role-play the self-assessment and comparison of collaborative assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

quiz.q: Your learner flew a solo practice session on Tuesday, and you give your critique at the next lesson on Friday. Which AIH guidance did you miss?
options: A critique should wait until the learner has fully reflected
A critique should be written so the learner keeps a record
A critique should come right after the performance is done
A critique should be given only in front of other learners
quiz.why: A critique should come immediately after the performance, while the details are easy to recall [[25:141|AIH 6-10]], and a solo debrief belongs right after the flight, while it is vivid [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Self-reflection belongs in the debrief, not days later, and a critique may be oral, written or both [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

quiz.q: In a debrief you tell your learner, 'Your holding entries weren't as good as last week.' Which characteristic of an effective critique does this lack most?
options: Specific
Flexible
Comprehensive
Thoughtful
quiz.why: Learners cannot act on a recommendation unless they know specifically what it is; the AIH's 'your second weld wasn't as good as your first' has little value. Say why and how to improve [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. Comprehensive is tempting, but a comprehensive critique need not be long or detailed [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

quiz.q: After a messy approach, you start your critique at the moment the learner went below the glidepath and work back through the steps that led there. Is this sound?
options: No; a critique must follow the order of the flight
Yes; working back from the failure is one AIH pattern
No; the AIH says to open every critique with a grade
Only in a written critique, never in an oral one
quiz.why: Almost any logical pattern works. The AIH names the sequence of the performance, starting where it failed and working backward, building around one glaring deficiency, and parts to whole [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. Flight order is only one of these options.

quiz.q: In ground school you ask one learner to lead the critique of a classmate's practice departure briefing. What does the AIH say about this method?
options: It is the most efficient method, since peers speak freely
It lets you stop controlling the process
It gives the performer a permanent record of all comments
It may be inefficient, but it can generate interest
quiz.why: A learner-led critique may not be efficient because the participants are inexperienced, but it can generate interest and learning [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. You keep firm control whenever learners take part, and the permanent record is an advantage of the written critique [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

quiz.q: Your class critique of a learner's weather briefing went well, but nobody noticed she never checked the freezing level. Ten minutes remain. What do you do?
options: Leave it; adding points undercuts the class's ownership
Assign it as homework so the critique ends on time
Cover it now, in the time saved for missed points
Ask the performer to grade the class
quiz.why: Save time at the end of the learner assessment for areas that were omitted, not emphasized enough, or worth repeating; you also correct erroneous impressions in any critique [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. Group ownership of the ideas is a benefit of learner participation [[25:141|AIH 6-10]], not a reason to leave a point out.

quiz.q: Your learner is on her third holding lesson. Which question best fits the AIH's characteristics of an effective oral question?
options: Do you understand the holding entries now?
Why did you choose a teardrop entry for this hold today?
Which entry did you fly, why, and how long were the legs?
What are the VFR weather minimums in Class E airspace?
quiz.why: Effective questions apply to the subject, are brief and clear, fit the learner's stage, center on one idea and present a challenge [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. The first is a yes/no question to avoid, the third mixes what, why and how long, and the fourth does not apply to the subject of instruction [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

quiz.q: You ask, 'On a nonprecision approach in a twin with the right engine out, a gusty tailwind, no heading indicator and the GPS in dead reckoning, what is your first action?' Which type of question to avoid is it most like?
options: Puzzle
Toss-up
Oversize
Irrelevant
quiz.why: The AIH's puzzle example piles conditions onto one landing: a conventional gear airplane, a weak brake, a crosswind, full flaps and a power-on wheel landing [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. An effective question centers on one idea [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. It is not a toss-up: the AIH's toss-up example forces a choice between two actions, squawking 7700 or picking a landing spot, and its oversize example asks what to do before an engine overhaul [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

quiz.q: A pre-solo learner asks how airline crews are approved to fly RNP approaches. A full answer would swamp her. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Answer it fully now to reward curiosity
Tell her it is not on her test, so it is not worth her time
Reverse the question so she works the answer out herself
Call it a good question and invite her to ask again later
quiz.why: When a full answer would bring in more than the learner needs now, say the question is good and pertinent, explain that a detailed answer would complicate the learning at this point, and invite it again at the right point in training [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. A reverse question returns it to the learner to answer [[25:214|AIH G-6]], which fails when she lacks the knowledge.

quiz.q: Your instrument learner asks how a certain autopilot mode captures the glideslope, and you are not sure. What do you do?
options: Guess confidently to keep her trust
Change the subject and quietly look it up after the flight
Admit you're not sure, then look it up together afterward
Tell her to ask the chief instructor, who knows the type
quiz.why: Freely admit not knowing, and promise to get the answer or help the learner look it up [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. Learners sense a bluff quickly, and it destroys their confidence in the instructor [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

quiz.q: Three instructors read your new stage test against the course objectives and rewrite or drop items that do not fit. Which test characteristic are they checking?
options: Reliability
Validity
Discrimination
Usability
quiz.why: Validity is the extent to which a test measures what it is supposed to measure; to estimate it, several instructors read the test against the objectives and change or drop items that do not pertain [[25:135|AIH 6-4]]. Reliability is consistency of results with repeated measurement [[25:135|AIH 6-4]].

quiz.q: A colleague's true-false items keep using 'always', 'never' and 'only'. What is the problem?
options: They lower objectivity, since graders read them differently
They make items too hard for the weaker learners in a class
Nothing, as long as each statement is entirely true or false
They are determiners, words that give learners clues to the answer
quiz.why: Absolutes such as all, every, only, no and never are determiners: they give clues to the answer, so avoid them [[25:198|AIH B-2]]. Because absolutes are rare, such words usually make the statement false [[25:210|AIH G-2]]. Making a statement entirely true or false is a separate guideline and does not remove the clue.

quiz.q: Your instrument learner flies approaches well and wants a checkride date. Per the AIH, what must you do before you recommend him?
options: Evaluate every task in the ACS or PTS against its standards
Check only his weak tasks, since the examiner picks a sample
Give a written test, because his flying is already logged
Rank his flying against your other learners before signing
quiz.why: Evaluators may cover every task, so evaluate all tasks before recommending; the check need not be formal but should follow criterion-referenced testing [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. A recommendation should never rest on less than the complete ACS/PTS procedure [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Ranking learners against each other is the opposite of criterion-referenced testing [[25:210|AIH G-2]].

quiz.q: In a collaborative assessment your learner rates his partial panel work 'Perform'. You saw your coaching correct his heading drift twice. What do you do?
options: Accept his rating, since a self-assessment is never overruled
Grade it a C and explain that Perform is the same as an A
Talk it through: needing coaching fits Practice on the rubric
Skip the discussion and write your own rating in his record
quiz.why: Practice means coaching corrects the deviations; Perform means the learner corrects his own errors without help [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. In the AIH example Linda and Brian talk through their different ratings until Brian sees where he needs practice, and the rubric must not be forced into A to F [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

final_quiz.q: An examiner asks how evaluation and critique differ for a learner just starting a new skill. Which answer fits the AIH?
options: A grade motivates a beginner more than any suggestion
A critique is formal and graded; evaluation is informal
A critique is used only after a stage check or practical test
Early on, practical suggestions help more than a grade does
final_quiz.why: In the initial stages of skill acquisition, practical suggestions are more valuable to the learner than a grade [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. The second option is backward: informal assessments can include verbal critique and are not part of the final grade [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

final_quiz.q: You like your learner and want her to pass the stage check, so you let a missed altimeter setting slide. What does the AIH call this?
options: Halo error
Flexibility
Discrimination
Recency
final_quiz.why: Sympathy or over-identification with a learner that influences objectivity is halo error; assess the facts of the performance as they were [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]. Flexibility means fitting tone, technique and content to the occasion, not overlooking facts [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

final_quiz.q: A new learner shrugs off your honest critique. Per the AIH, what makes an assessment acceptable to a learner?
options: Your flight instructor certificate, which sets your authority
Confidence in your competence, sincerity and teaching ability
Grading easily for a few lessons until the learner trusts you
Letting the learner pick the standards for the next lesson
final_quiz.why: Learners need confidence in the instructor's qualifications, teaching ability, sincerity, competence and authority; a certificate or credential alone rarely suffices [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]. Easy grading would break objectivity [[25:133|AIH 6-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your debrief walks through 14 small errors in detail. What does the AIH say about a comprehensive critique?
options: It covers every error, so a long list is the right approach
It covers only weaknesses, since strengths need no comment
It need not be long; pick the few points that help the most
It applies only to written tests, not to oral critiques
final_quiz.why: A comprehensive assessment is not necessarily long and need not treat every aspect in detail; it includes strengths and weaknesses, and you decide whether a few major points or a number of minor points help more [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].

final_quiz.q: Why might you ask every learner in a ground class to write a critique of one learner's presentation?
options: So the rest of the class benefits from hearing every comment
Because it takes less thought than an oral one
Because it replaces your control and supervision of the critique
So the performer keeps a record of everyone's suggestions
final_quiz.why: A written critique allows more time and thought, gives learners a record to keep and, when all learners write one, gives the performer a permanent record of everyone's suggestions. Its drawback is that the other class members do not benefit [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your instrument learner, now well along in training, wants to run the postflight review herself. What does the AIH support?
options: Let her lead while you guide it with targeted questions
Decline, because the critique is the instructor's job alone
Let her lead and stay silent so you do not bias her review
Have her write it up at home and skip the discussion
final_quiz.why: As the learner grows in flight knowledge, he or she should be able to lead the postflight review while the instructor guides the discussion with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. Even a self-critique stays under the instructor's control and supervision [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner can name every symbol on an approach chart but cannot explain why two approaches to the same runway have different minimums. Which questions should you add?
options: More fact questions, to build recall before anything else
HOTS questions that ask why or how and require analysis
Yes/no questions, to check confidence quickly
Toss-up questions, to force a choice between answers
final_quiz.why: Fact questions rely on recall; HOTS questions ask why or how and make the learner analyze and draw conclusions [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. Most aviation training is at the understanding level or higher, so questions should infer cause and effect [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]. Yes/no and toss-up questions are types to avoid [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

final_quiz.q: At the end of your briefing you ask, 'Any questions?' and your learner says no. Why does the AIH discourage relying on this?
options: It is a puzzle question that piles on too many conditions
It is a toss-up between two answers that may both be right
It is a yes/no question that shows you very little
It is a trick question, a battle of wits
final_quiz.why: Effective quizzing does not include yes/no questions such as 'Do you understand?' or 'Do you have any questions?' [[25:142|AIH 6-11]], and closed-ended questions check only the rote level [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Inviting questions before leaving the explanation phase is still good practice [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]; the problem is using it as your check of understanding.

final_quiz.q: During a debrief your learner asks a long, tangled question and you are not sure what he means. What is your first step?
options: Answer the part you understood and move on
Ask him to write it down for the next lesson
Pass it to another learner to answer for him
Confirm what he means by paraphrasing it
final_quiz.why: First be sure you clearly understand the question before attempting to answer [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. Paraphrasing shows the learner what his statement meant to you, so he can correct or expand it [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: On a presolo test you want to see whether the learner can explain the traffic pattern procedures in her own words. Which item type fits?
options: Supply type, where she writes her own answer
True-false, since it measures understanding best
Matching, since it removes guessing entirely
Multiple choice with five or more alternatives
final_quiz.why: Supply-type items let the learner organize knowledge and express ideas, and on a presolo test they help show whether the learner knows the procedures [[25:197|AIH B-1]]. True-false items are generally not considered valid [[25:198|AIH B-2]], matching reduces guessing rather than removing it [[25:201|AIH B-5]], and more than four convincing alternatives is hard to write [[25:199|AIH B-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your student pilot has finished the presolo knowledge test. What does 14 CFR 61.87 require before you authorize solo?
options: A second instructor must grade it independently
You must review every incorrect answer with the student
The student must retake it until scoring 100 percent
The test must be sent to the FAA for its records
final_quiz.why: The authorized instructor must administer the test and, at its conclusion, review all incorrect answers with the student before authorizing solo [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(b)]]. The rule sets no second grader, no 100 percent score and no FAA submission.

final_quiz.q: Your multiple choice distractors are answers no learner would ever pick. What does the AIH suggest instead?
options: Add more alternatives until one of them looks attractive
Make the correct answer the longest one every time
Use common learner errors as the distractors
Write each distractor as a trick to catch careless readers
final_quiz.why: An effective way to divert learners who have not mastered the subject is to use common learner errors as distractors [[25:199|AIH B-3]]. More than four convincing alternatives is hard to write [[25:199|AIH B-3]], trick questions should be avoided [[25:200|AIH B-4]], and a correct answer that is always the longest repeats a pattern the AIH found in instructor-made tests [[25:201|AIH B-5]], letting learners pick it without knowing it is correct [[25:199|AIH B-3]].

final_quiz.q: Per AC 61-65K, what does the ACS do that the PTS does not?
options: Replaces the practical test with a written examination
Drops oral questioning in favor of flight performance
Ranks applicants against each other instead of a standard
Evaluates knowledge, risk management and skill elements
final_quiz.why: The ACS evaluates knowledge, risk management and skill elements for each task, and each element says whether it is evaluated orally or by performance [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.3]]. The examiner may use oral testing at any time [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.1]], and both standards are criterion referenced [[25:140|AIH 6-9]].

final_quiz.q: A CFI uses the PTS task list as the lesson plan for every flight and trains exactly to its tolerances. What does the AIH say?
options: The PTS is a testing tool; lessons should build to or past it
Correct: the PTS is the complete syllabus
Correct, as long as each learner keeps passing the stage checks
Only the ACS, not the PTS, may be used as a lesson plan this way
final_quiz.why: The ACS/PTS is not a teaching tool but a testing tool, and lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed it before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. The standards cover only the most critical job tasks, not an entire syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

final_quiz.q: You give a pilot an IPC and the performance is unsatisfactory. What does AC 61-98E recommend?
options: Endorse it, with a note listing the weak areas
No endorsement; log the session as dual instruction given
Endorse it if the pilot promises more training soon
Sign it, since an IPC is a review, not a test
final_quiz.why: The instructor should not endorse an unsatisfactory IPC and should log the session as dual instruction given [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]]. Either way, give the pilot a comprehensive analysis with suggestions for the weak areas [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4]].

final_quiz.q: On your CFII practical test, which Area I tasks will the examiner certainly evaluate?
options: Only the one task the examiner picks
All seven tasks, since every task must be tested
Tasks E, F and G, and at least one other Area I task
Whichever tasks you missed on the FOI knowledge test
final_quiz.why: Flight instructor applicants are evaluated on one or more tasks in each area, and required tasks are named in a note after the area title [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. In the CFII PTS the Area I note requires at least Tasks E, F and G and one other task (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I NOTE).

final_quiz.q: In scenario-based training, when does the AIH say to use collaborative assessment?
options: Only at the end of a course, as the final grade
Only after a failed stage check, to find the cause
Only for ground lessons
Whenever the learner has completed a training scenario
final_quiz.why: With SBT, collaborative assessment is used whenever the learner has completed a scenario, during the postflight evaluation [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. It evaluates whether certain learning criteria were met during the SBT [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

takeaways: The PTS says critique and evaluation; the current AIH says assessment. Know both and connect them.
A critique exists to improve performance: right after the flight, good and bad, parts and whole.
Eight characteristics: objective, flexible, acceptable, comprehensive, constructive, organized, thoughtful, specific.
Six methods, one set of ground rules: you keep control, settle disagreements, protect the performer and save time to close.
Ask one-idea, challenging why and how questions; never rely on 'Do you understand?'
Answer directly, check the learner is satisfied, defer what is too advanced, and never bluff.
Build tests from objectives to criterion-referenced items, and make validity your first check.
The PTS and ACS are criterion-referenced testing tools, not a syllabus: evaluate every task before you sign, and let the learner self-assess first.
cfi_notes: How it is tested: the CFII PTS makes this Task required on every FOI evaluation: the evaluator selects at least Tasks E, F and G and one other (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I NOTE). The objective verb is 'explaining', and evaluators are told to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions when possible (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Have one learner story ready for each element.

Terms: the PTS lists FAA-H-8083-9 as the reference and uses 'critique', 'evaluation' and 'student', but tells users to reference the current edition of each document (FAA-S-8081-9E, references NOTE). The current AIH says assessment and learner [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. Use the PTS word to show you heard the question, then answer in the AIH's words.

'Ground rules for a critique' is not a heading in the current AIH. The rules in this lesson come from AIH 6-10 [[25:141|AIH 6-10]] and from guidance on AIH 3-13, 6-3, 8-2, 8-4 and 9-6. If the examiner asks, say where each rule comes from.

AC 61-98E says the AIH's Chapter 5, The Teaching Process, gives suggestions for the postflight 'collaborative critique' after an IPC [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4]], but in FAA-H-8083-9B the collaborative critique is in Chapter 6, Assessment [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. Teach from Chapter 6.

The AIH says a practical test recommendation on FAA Form 8710-1 is valid for 60 days [[25:183|AIH 9-13]], while 14 CFR 61.39 requires training within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)(i)]], as AC 61-65K restates [[12:10|AC 61-65K 14]]. Teach the regulation; the 60-day figure in the rules is the credit period after a discontinued practical test [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.5.1]].

SRM rubric wording varies: AIH 6-6 gives explain, practice and manage-decide [[25:137|AIH 6-6]], AIH 1-28 adds not observed as a fourth component, and both progression examples start SRM at 'describe' [[25:32|AIH 1-28]] [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Use the three-level rubric plus not observed, and treat 'describe' as informal wording.

Overlap with other FOI Tasks: 'review and evaluation of student performance' is also an item of Task C, and student evaluation and practical test recommendations belong to Task F (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I). In this Task, stay on the methods: how to critique, question, test and grade.

Learner-centered grading is checked beyond this Task: the PTS lists the ability to use learner-centered grading and debriefing techniques among the evaluator's checks, and, under satisfactory performance, knowledge of the development and use of a course of training, syllabus and lesson plan, including scenario-based training and collaborative assessment (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Debrief each maneuver the examiner flies as your 'student' the same way.

As a flight instructor, you may give an IPC only with an instrument rating on your pilot and flight instructor certificates appropriate to the aircraft [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]], and it is tied to the instrument ACS or PTS task table [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]]. It is a ready CFII example when the examiner asks for uses of performance tests.
gaps: No source gives a pass mark for an instructor-made test; the AIH's 70 percent is only an example criterion objective for a quiz [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Your syllabus sets the real standard.
No source says how long a postflight critique should take or how many points it should cover; the AIH says only that a comprehensive critique is not necessarily long [[25:134|AIH 6-3]].
The AIH says selection items are well adapted to statistical item analysis [[25:197|AIH B-1]] but gives no method for doing one.

The sources do not say what to do if a learner still disagrees after the comparison in collaborative assessment; the AIH says only that you resolve disagreements in critiques [[25:141|AIH 6-10]] and that you and the learner jointly determine progress [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].
No source here gives the instrument ACS tolerances or the IPC task table itself; read them in FAA-S-ACS-8 [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1]].

activities.title: Which characteristic is it?
activities.intro: Tap what the instructor does, then the characteristic of an effective critique it shows.

pairs.l: Waits until the other learners leave before discussing the hard landing
Says exactly why the hold drifted and how to fix the wind correction
Grades the flight that happened, not the one the learner meant to fly
Fits tone and content to a strong learner's unusually poor flight
Pairs each weak point with a way to improve and skips empty praise
Starts where the approach fell apart and works back to the cause

activities.title: Which critique method?
activities.intro: Tap a description, then the critique method it belongs to.

items.t: You lead a discussion and invite the class to comment
Must never become a random free-for-all
One learner leads; you may set the pattern
May not be efficient, but can build interest
Teams each analyze one area and report back
One classmate presents the entire assessment
The learner assesses her own performance under your supervision
The performer keeps everyone's comments as a record
Its drawback: the rest of the class does not benefit

activities.title: True or false: ground rules for a critique
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A critique should wait until the next lesson so the learner can cool off.
cards.why: False. It should come immediately after the performance, while the details are easy to recall [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

cards.s: In any critique, the instructor resolves disagreements and corrects erroneous impressions.
A learner-led critique lets the instructor give up control of the process.
cards.why: False. Whenever learners take part, the instructor keeps firm control [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

cards.s: The instructor makes allowances for the learners' relative inexperience.
Inventing a few faults keeps a fast learner from getting overconfident.
cards.why: False. Deficiencies should not be invented; unfair criticism destroys confidence. Raise the standard instead [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

cards.s: If possible, avoid ending the evaluation on a negative note.
When time is short, telling a learner 'that was unsatisfactory' is enough.
cards.why: False. Errors must be identified and explained with how to correct them, or frustration follows [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

cards.s: Praise given too freely loses its value.

activities.title: Ground school night
activities.intro: You teach a two-hour instrument ground school on holding to six learners. Make each call.

steps.s: Halfway through, you want to check whether the class followed the entry procedures.
options: Ask, 'Does everyone understand the entries?'
Ask, 'How would you pick the entry for this hold?'
Ask about entries, timing, speeds and reports at once
Ask, 'Is a teardrop entry ever used, yes or no?'
steps.why: An effective question applies to the subject, is brief and clear, centers on one idea and presents a challenge; yes/no questions are to be avoided [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

steps.s: A learner asks how holding airspace is designed to protect against obstacles. A full answer would take twenty minutes and goes well beyond what the class needs at this point in training.
options: Answer it fully now so curiosity is rewarded
Tell the learner it is not on the knowledge test
Call it a good question and invite it again later
Ignore it and keep moving to protect the schedule
steps.why: Explain that the question is good and pertinent but a detailed answer now would complicate the learning, and invite it again at the right point in training [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

steps.s: Another learner asks about a holding rule you are not sure of.
options: Give your best recollection with confidence
Admit it and look it up together in the references
Say it is rarely tested and move on
Tell the learner to research it alone
steps.why: Freely admit not knowing and offer to help look it up [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]; a bluff destroys learner confidence [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

steps.s: You have just answered a learner's question about holding speeds.
options: Move straight on to keep the lesson's pace
Ask, 'Does that make sense?' and move on
Check that the learner is satisfied with it
Repeat the answer twice so it sticks
steps.why: After responding, find out whether the learner is satisfied with the answer [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]; a yes/no 'does that make sense?' reveals little [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. Application: have the learner apply it to the next example.

steps.s: You want every learner thinking about a new hold before anyone answers, then you want to hear from the quietest one.
options: Ask an overhead question, then a direct one
Ask a rhetorical question and answer it yourself
Call on the quiet learner first, with no warning
Ask a trick question to wake the group up
steps.why: An overhead question goes to the whole group to stimulate thought [[25:213|AIH G-5]], and a direct question is aimed at one person [[25:210|AIH G-2]]. A rhetorical question is normally answered by the instructor [[25:214|AIH G-6]], and trick questions are to be avoided [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

activities.title: Parts of a multiple choice item
activities.intro: Drag each piece of AIH test-writing guidance to the part of the sample item it describes.

pins.label: States the central problem, with only relevant material
A true compass error, but not the one the stem asks for
Wrong answer meant to attract a learner who lacks the knowledge
Keyed response: correct and impossible to refute

activities.why: From AIH Figure B-2: the stem sets the stage and holds only relevant material [[25:200|AIH B-4]]; the correct response must not be refutable, and distractors must attract learners who lack the knowledge [[25:199|AIH B-3]]. Variation is the difference between true and magnetic directions because the magnetic pole is not at the geographic pole, while deviation comes from magnetic fields in the aircraft [[23:107|IFH 5-12]]; a true statement that does not answer the problem is a popular kind of distractor [[25:201|AIH B-5]].

activities.title: PTS, ACS or both?
activities.intro: Tap a statement, then the standard it describes.

items.t: Evaluates knowledge, risk management and skill elements for each task
Each element says whether it is evaluated orally or by performance
Integrates risk management throughout, with appendix information
Used for the instrument rating, airplane: FAA-S-ACS-8
FAA-S-8081-9E, the standard for your CFII practical test
Criterion referenced: every successful applicant meets the standard
A testing document, not a teaching document
Areas of operation in a logical sequence, made up of tasks

activities.why: From [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.3]], [[25:164|AIH 8-6]], [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1]], [[25:140|AIH 6-9]] and [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. FAA-S-8081-9E is the Flight Instructor Instrument Practical Test Standards.

activities.title: Run an IPC as a performance test
activities.intro: Put the AC 61-98E steps for an instrument proficiency check in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Discuss the operating conditions and build a scenario-based plan of action
Agree with the pilot how you will conduct it and review the criteria for satisfactory completion
Check IFR knowledge: regulations, charts, weather, systems and ATC procedures
Have the pilot plan the flight, get weather, file and preflight
Fly the required tasks from the instrument ACS or PTS, plus any you choose
Debrief with a comprehensive analysis and suggestions, then endorse or log dual instruction

activities.title: Debrief after a partial panel lesson
activities.intro: Your instrument learner Sam just flew partial panel holds and an approach. Make each call in the debrief.

steps.s: You land and shut down. When do you debrief?
options: Right away, while the details are fresh
Tomorrow, after Sam has rested and reflected
At the start of the next lesson, as a review
After Sam writes a self-assessment at home
steps.why: A critique should come immediately after the performance, while the details are easy to recall [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

options: Read Sam your notes on every error in flight order
Give Sam a letter grade for the whole lesson
Ask Sam to replay the flight in his own words
Ask, 'Did that go well, yes or no?'
steps.why: Collaborative assessment starts with the learner's self-assessment, beginning with a replay of the flight [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Yes/no questions are to be avoided [[25:142|AIH 6-11]].

steps.s: Sam calls the partial panel approach 'perfect'. You had to coach him back on course twice.
options: Accept 'perfect' so Sam keeps his confidence
Compare: needing coaching puts it at Practice
Tell Sam he failed the approach
Skip it and move on to the next item
steps.why: Practice means coaching corrects the deviations [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]; compare the ratings in discussion, and remember the learner cannot flunk a lesson [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

steps.s: Sam asks why he kept chasing the VSI. You know the answer well.
options: Tell him to look it up for homework
Give a long lecture on every instrument
Say it does not matter as long as he improves
Answer directly, then check he is satisfied
